newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway, Egypt see crucial test for peace process.
newsitem.headline: Norway, Egypt see crucial test for peace process.

text.p: Norway and Egypt were cautiously optimistic on Thursday of a revival in the Middle East peace process, following landmark talks between the Israeli and Palestinian leaders.
But both countries said they saw a difficult path ahead despite Wednesday's brief summit between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"While welcoming the events of yesterday, it remains to be seen whether this is just a photo opportunity or a serious beginning to getting the talks back on track," said Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa during a visit to Oslo.
"Perhaps there is a glimpse of hope nowadays, but the test will be the actual implementation of the agreements."
Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal said he saw no alternative but to try to steer the Israelis and Palestinians back onto the negotiating track.

"We have shared our concern with the new government in Israel and we have tried to engage them in a dialogue in how to move on...I'm not particularly optimistic, but I think there is no alternative to the peace process," Godal said.
Norway hosted 14 secret meetings between Israeli and PLO negotiators in 1993 that led to the PLO-Israeli peace pact.
The Egyptian arrived from Paris on Wednesday for a two-day visit to meet Godal and Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland.
Egypt on Sunday said it was giving Israel three weeks to start implementing PLO-Israel peace deals or it would cancel a Middle East economic conference planned for Egypt in November.

The deals, signed in interim peace agreements between the former Israeli centre-left government and the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO), set up the expanded self-rule area in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Netanyahu's conservative government was elected in May on a pledge not to swap occupied Arab land for peace.
"There is a lot the Israeli government has to do to establish a comprehensive and fair peace," the Egyptian foreign minister said.

"We cannot continue seriously while settlements are being built or Palestinian territories are being confiscated. No withdrawal from Hebron...means no honouring of the previous agreements, agreements signed by the previous government, as if the previous government in Israel was illegal."
He said there was a possibility of a settlement "providing Mr Netanyahu changes his policies and attitudes."
